description: Talks from Objective by the Sea v4.0 (2021).

talks.title: Siri, Find My Ex
talks.teaser: Shows how stalkerware and Apple's AirTag enable intimate partner abuse, and where current mitigations fall short.
talks.summary:
Eva Galperin, director of cybersecurity at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, argues that for survivors of intimate partner abuse, surveillance often begins at home. Abusers typically have physical access to a victim's devices and intimate knowledge of their routines. She explains how commercial stalkerware hides on phones and how abusers obtain Apple ID credentials, often by coercion, so that stalkerware services can pull iCloud backup data and show it in a web portal.

She reviews Apple's iCloud restrictions and two-factor authentication, which block most backup retrieval, and cites a test of popular stalkerware products where few could pull data from iCloud. Older approaches such as WebWatcher, which depends on local iTunes Wi-Fi sync, are easier to detect. Galperin praises Apple's guide for reviewing device and account settings. The central focus is the AirTag. Its Find My network turns nearby iPhones into a tracking mesh, yet the anti-stalking safeguards are weak: an alert sound that is easily muffled, no Android alert at launch, and a reset timer that dropped from three days to one, which an abuser living with a victim can easily keep resetting.

She closes by describing IBM's principles for building products resistant to abuse: diverse teams, privacy and user control, reliable activity logs, strong security, and intuitive design. Her point is that Apple's blind spot was users outside its ecosystem. For practitioners, the takeaways are to check device and account access with people at risk, and to test new products against the abuse case, especially as connected devices spread.

talks.title: Plug-n-Play: Using Native Code with Installer Plugins for Initial Access
talks.teaser: Covers macOS installer plugins as a native code route for initial access, and how Apple's changes shorten their process lifetime.

talks.title: Made In America: Analyzing US Spy Agencies macOS Implants
talks.teaser: Walks through two leaked macOS implants tied to the CIA and NSA, covering triage, string decryption, and remote tasking logic.
talks.summary:
Runa Sandvik and Patrick Wardle examine two macOS implants leaked between 2015 and 2017: Green Lambert, linked to the CIA's Lamberts family, and Double Fantasy, linked to the NSA. They present the samples as old artifacts whose study shows how sophisticated operators build and engineer their tools.

Sandvik starts with Green Lambert. She ties its development documents to reporting from Symantec and Kaspersky, then does static triage, reviews the symbols to work out which OS release it needs, and runs it on an old Lion system. She covers persistence through a launch agent, how its behaviour changes when offline, and how she recovered command-line arguments and encrypted strings using Hopper and LLDB. A certificate history for its command domain helps place activity around 2007 to 2013.

Wardle then covers Double Fantasy, a first-stage implant. He writes a Hopper script to find and decrypt its embedded strings, which reveals command-line flags, a configuration format and a survey routine that he runs in a debugger. He also maps a jump table of remote commands, including a download-and-execute command that clears DYLD variables first. The practical takeaway is that the same workflow applies to any macOS malware, and that the samples show careful engineering such as proper daemonization and support for authenticating proxies.

talks.title: Mac Detections by The Numbers
talks.teaser: Walks through Mac malware and adware detection data, showing where each sample appeared and what stood out.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with Malwarebytes detection totals for 2021, which stayed fairly steady across the year, and shows where those detections were seen. The United States dominates, mirroring the company's customer base, while Asia is thinly represented, so regional figures carry that bias. Potentially unwanted programs and adware, led by bundled installers from one vendor, make up most of the volume.

The middle of the talk covers individual samples. A generic suspicious-behavior rule caught many launch agents and daemons with random names, often containing curl-to-bash pipelines or base64-encoded Python, and that activity declined over the year. Detection geography varied: XCSSET and OSAMiner leaned toward the Middle East and Asia, while ElectroRAT and Electrum Stealer had very few sightings. Silver Sparrow's empty ._insu file inflated its counts, and excluding it shrank the spike considerably. XcodeSpy, WildPython and XLoader showed little or no real-world detection, which may reflect targeting outside the customer base.

The closing takeaway is that regional spread often matches the region where an actor operates, though visibility gaps make that hard to confirm. The speaker stresses that adware and unwanted programs remain the everyday threat to Mac users, far outweighing nation-state tooling in volume.

talks.title: Becoming a Yogi on Mac ATT&CK with OceanLotus Postures
talks.teaser: Shows how MITRE ATT&CK for macOS can structure OceanLotus threat intelligence, hunting and emulation work.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the common belief that MITRE ATT&CK only covers Windows. The presenters explain that its macOS matrix has existed since 2017 and describe how the framework is organized: tactics as adversary goals, techniques beneath them, and sub-techniques where operating system specifics usually live. Each entry carries a description, metadata, real-world procedure examples, detection ideas and references. They note that public reporting on macOS malware is thin, so much of the detail comes from community researchers.

Using the OceanLotus group as a case study, the speakers show how threat intelligence maps onto techniques, both from published reports and from malware samples attributed to the actor. They break a shell script into the behaviors it performs and match each one to an ATT&CK technique. They then cover threat hunting, pairing techniques with the data sources that would reveal them, and emulation, where existing plans and open-source tools can reproduce the same behaviors. Open reporting carries biases, so they stress adding an organization's own telemetry and internal intelligence.

The closing section compares what a team can currently see with what intelligence says adversaries do, to find gaps and set priorities. Responses may be new detections, data collection, user training, or accepted risk rather than only technical controls, and emulation is used to validate results. The main takeaway is a shared vocabulary across teams. The presenters also asked practitioners to share macOS findings so the framework can keep improving, and noted that automatically mapping reports to techniques is still an unsolved problem.

talks.title: Pocket Litter - A Peek Inside Your Apple Wallet
talks.teaser: Maps what Apple Wallet stores on iOS and macOS, from passes and transactions to Apple Cash and transit trips.
talks.summary:
Sarah Edwards, a digital forensics researcher, walks through the data Apple Wallet keeps on Apple devices and why that data matters in investigations. She starts by separating the related terms: Wallet is the app, Apple Pay is the payment technology, Apple Cash is a digital debit option, and Apple Card is the credit product. She then explains where passes such as tickets, boarding passes and loyalty cards live, how each one is packaged as a directory with a JSON file holding its details, and how iCloud can sync them to other devices.

The core of the talk is a large SQLite database that holds payment cards, Apple Cash peer payments, daily cash rewards, transit taps and Apple Card transactions. She shows how timestamps, merchant records and location tables can be joined to rebuild a timeline of a person's spending and movements, and how those results can be cross-checked against messages or emailed receipts. She notes that full card numbers are not stored, while the schema itself is hard to read, with many opaque table and column names that have to be worked out through testing.

She closes with sync behavior: Apple Card transactions spread widely across devices, while other card transactions tend to remain on the device where they were made, and transit data is kept per device. Practitioners should expect access to depend on backups, full file system extractions and device encryption, and should treat these stores as a rich source of personal context.

talks.title: Kernel Exploitation on Apple's M1 chip
talks.teaser: Shows how a kernel driver on Apple M1 Macs was exploited after Apple's earlier patches fell short.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the Apple Video Encoder kernel driver, AppleAVE2, which runs in kernel space on iOS devices and, from the M1 generation, on Macs. The speaker explains why its complex code and heavy user-kernel memory mapping make it an attractive target. The driver first drew attention in 2017, when earlier research exposed simple flaws that Apple then patched.

The middle of the talk covers the speaker's own findings against the newer macOS build. These include an overflow missing a size boundary check and a race condition involving shared memory, both of which can be turned into kernel read and write primitives. The speaker compares how Apple addressed each bug, noting that the race fix added a buffer around part of the mapped memory while the overflow was handled differently. The argument is that minimal patches are common because thorough fixes take much more effort, so researchers should examine how their reports were actually fixed.

The closing section describes the speaker's experience with Apple's security bounty, including slow communication and a payout of about $52,000, and compares it with other disclosure programs. It also contrasts sandbox-reachable attack surface with externally reachable methods that need no sandbox escape, and briefly describes a race-based driver bug that can map physical memory. The talk ends with the view that macOS hardening has improved year after year, especially in the kernel.

talks.title: n-1 and n-2: Should we really trust in you?
talks.teaser: Compares macOS security patch coverage across supported releases and asks whether older versions stay as safe as the newest.
talks.summary:
The talk examines Apple's practice of patching the current and two previous macOS releases and asks whether an older version is really as safe as the newest one. Apple rarely publishes which versions each fix reaches, so the speaker had to infer coverage from public advisories and from the researchers who reported the bugs.

Using data from every macOS security advisory since Big Sur shipped, the speaker counted 468 patched vulnerabilities and sorted them by which supported releases received each fix. Many were patched everywhere, but a notable group reached only some versions, and a few appeared in the oldest supported release without the middle one. Of 15 bugs Apple flagged as possibly exploited in the wild, several were fixed only for Big Sur. A WebKit flaw used by the Pegasus spyware was patched for Big Sur and Catalina but remained open on Mojave, a gap an outside researcher confirmed. Earlier examples such as the High Sierra root login bug and the Go to Fail SSL flaw showed that new releases can also ship serious mistakes. iOS patch coverage was compared as well.

The main takeaway is that the newest macOS is generally the safest, since it receives the most fixes and the most important ones. Users who must stay on an older release should avoid using it as their primary or internet-facing machine, and consider keeping it offline for legacy apps. The speaker promised a white paper with fuller details.

talks.title: Environmental Disaster: A LaunchServices Tale
talks.teaser: Shows how a LaunchServices logic flaw let a sandboxed macOS app escape the App Sandbox in several ways.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a refresher on the macOS App Sandbox, which is meant to contain apps installed from the Mac App Store and limit damage from compromised apps. It explains why the ability to start other applications through Launch Services is a notable gap, since launched apps do not inherit the sandbox. The speaker traces how an open request moves from the framework to the Core Services UI agent and then to the process-launching daemons.

The core problem is that a sandboxed app can set environment variables on an unsandboxed application it launches. The speaker shows several ways this was abused: injecting a dynamic library into a scripting host, redirecting the home directory so a plugin loader reads from a path inside a sandbox container, and using a deprecated API to launch a Perl interpreter whose debug mode runs attacker-supplied code. An Electron app was also targeted through Node options. Each vector was addressed by a separate patch across several macOS releases, and the speaker argues the underlying design issue remains.

For defenders, the talk offers detection heuristics. These include flagging unsandboxed processes whose home variable points into another app's sandbox container, watching Electron apps launched with run-as-node settings, and treating a sandboxed parent that launches an unsandboxed child through Launch Services as suspicious. Developers are advised to avoid naming apps in ways that match Electron's own binary and to disable the run-as-node fuse. The speaker also released a tool for reversing recent macOS private frameworks.

talks.title: All Your Macs Are Belong To Us
talks.teaser: Explains how a logic flaw in macOS policy code let unsigned apps bypass Gatekeeper, and how it was exploited as a zero-day.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the macOS security stack, covering file quarantine, Gatekeeper, notarization, XProtect and TCC, and explains why Gatekeeper is the main obstacle for red teams. The speakers then describe CVE-2021-30657, found by Cedric Owens. A bare app bundle with a script as its main executable and no Info.plist file could be launched with a double-click, skipping the usual checks. Apple fixed the issue within days in Big Sur 11.3 and Catalina.

Patrick Wardle traces the root cause. By comparing system logs from three unsigned test apps, he narrowed the problem to sysPolicyd, the policy daemon. Reversing its closed-source binary showed that a bundle-classification routine treated a script-based app without Info.plist as not being a bundle. Gatekeeper then returned an evaluation type that allowed execution. Jaron Bradley explains how Jamf Protect built a behavioral detection for this pattern. That detection caught the Shlayer adware family abusing the flaw as a zero-day, and the authors rapidly altered their samples after XProtect added a signature.

Wardle also presents a prevention approach. It uses Endpoint Security to hold new process launches that were translocated from the internet and are not notarized, and he implemented it in his open-source BlockBlock tool. Finally, diffing the unpatched and patched sysPolicyd showed that Apple added checks for a .app extension and a Contents/MacOS directory. The takeaway is that macOS policy code contained shallow logic bugs that had gone unaudited.

talks.title: Mount(ain) of Bugs
talks.teaser: Explores how macOS mount operations enable privilege escalation and privacy bypasses, from kernel MAC hooks to real exploits.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through how macOS mounts volumes and how the kernel's mandatory access control framework hooks into the mount system calls. It explains that the disk arbitration service runs as root and is reachable from sandboxed applications, so it performs mounts on behalf of callers and depends on its own ownership and sandbox checks.

The middle section reviews past macOS bugs where mounting was central. These include an authorization reference exposed through a predictable temporary directory that could be replaced with a RAM disk, a time-of-check to time-of-use race in the disk arbitration service that allowed mounting over root-owned paths, and a snapshot mount that bypassed privacy controls. Further cases cover replacing the privacy database with a disk image, abusing the app translocation service to read protected folders, and mounting over predictable installer temp paths to reach root code execution through periodic scripts.

The closing part notes that several issues were addressed by adding sandbox checks, requiring file descriptors, or tying snapshot mounts to full disk access, though some of these design choices remain contested. The Q&A touches on the speaker's experience with Apple's bug bounty program, describing long waits and uneven communication. The takeaway for practitioners is that mount operations are a powerful primitive for both privilege escalation and privacy bypass, and that any privileged process trusting a user-controlled path deserves close review.

talks.title: The Wild World of macOS Installers
talks.teaser: Shows how macOS packages, disk images and developer libraries get abused to run code, with detection ideas.
talks.summary:
Tony Lambert of Red Canary opens by defining an installer broadly as anything that writes executable code to disk, and notes that on macOS the gap between an installer and malware is mostly a matter of trust. He walks through the platform's installer components, including the command-line installer, the GUI installer that launches from launchd, and installd, which stages payloads in randomized sandbox folders before merging them into the file system.

The middle of the talk covers where code can hide. Package pre- and postinstall scripts can be written in shell, Python, Perl or even compiled binaries, and some packages contain no payload at all, only scripts that fetch content later. Distribution XML can call system.run to execute commands with root privileges, and disk images mounted under volumes with misleading names like player or installer are common. For developer libraries, he showed how setup.py in pip, version.rb in RubyGems and npm install scripts can run arbitrary code at install time, with persistence and extra downloads as the main red flags.

For defenders, he suggested hunting for unusual child processes of the installer and package script services, watching for hdiutil attach activity, and flagging installs that write launch agents or shell profiles. He acknowledged that legitimate packaging varies so widely that the signal is noisy, and cautioned against trusting logos or branding, since lookalike assets are common. Checking the vendor's code signature is the more reliable step, though he noted that malicious actors still obtain signing certificates.

talks.title: FIDO on MacOS: How it works, Attack Vectors and Other Learnings
talks.teaser: Shows how WebAuthn and FIDO work on macOS and how a browser extension can interfere with registration and login.
talks.summary:
Joel Rennich, who works on Mac authentication at Jamf, opens by framing FIDO and WebAuthn as a strong login option with rough edges worth understanding. He splits the model into three parts: the relying party, such as a website or identity provider, the platform, usually the browser, and the authenticator, which is either an external hardware key or Touch ID and Face ID on a Mac. He covers protocol details such as credential ID lengths and signature counters, and shows that Chrome and Safari behave differently, with Chrome producing 80-byte IDs and Safari returning zeroed counters.

The middle of the talk covers interfering with the flow. A browser extension can wrap the credential create and get functions, log the requests and responses, and modify them before the browser acts on them. Rennich demonstrates converting a platform authenticator request into a cross-platform one and inserting an attestation object. Using a software key he built, he gets past a Cloudflare challenge that expects attestation, and enrolls and signs in to an Okta test account without touching a hardware device. He also notes that Apple's synced platform keys in iCloud Keychain blur the platform and cross-platform categories that some services rely on.

For defenders, the takeaway is that user presence and key possession do not prove the browser was honest. Attestation can help filter out unknown keys, but built-in Safari and Chrome authenticators do not supply it, and requiring it in services such as Azure carries usability trade-offs. Rennich suggests treating the browser as part of the trust boundary, weighing attestation requirements against who can still sign in, and continuing to prefer FIDO over passwords.

talks.title: iOS Reverse Engineering With Frida
talks.teaser: Shows how to set up Frida on a jailbroken iPhone and use it to hook and trace running iOS processes.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Frida, a dynamic instrumentation toolkit that injects JavaScript into running native processes, and argues that iOS reverse engineering is approachable with a computer and a jailbroken iPhone. The speaker walks through preparing the environment: installing matching Frida versions on the host and the device, choosing a jailbreak based on the phone's chip and iOS version, and adding Frida from a package source on the device.

The core of the talk covers three methodologies. Connect and explore uses the command line to list loaded modules, filter them for libraries of interest, find base addresses, and inspect memory ranges, along with loading scripts from files. Catch and release uses frida-trace to hook Objective-C and plain C functions, and shows why the correct flag matters. The speaker applies this to the Messages process to follow a PDF-rendering path in CoreGraphics tied to a published zero-click exploit, then uses a back trace to display the call chain. The Python bindings are presented as a clearer way to pass and handle data, such as memory dumps, than JavaScript.

The closing tips cover case-insensitive matching to widen hook coverage, a no-pause flag that avoids reconnecting, and spawn gating for short-lived processes that cannot otherwise be attached to. The talk ends by noting that Frida is free and open source, and that bug reports and contributions are welcome.

talks.title: Anti Analysis Logic of Arm Malware on macOS
talks.teaser: Walks through arm64 reversing basics and the anti-debugging and anti-VM checks in an early Apple Silicon Mac malware sample.
talks.summary:
Apple's M1 chips run native arm64 code, so malware compiled for them is becoming a real concern on macOS. The talk explains how universal binaries carry both Intel and arm64 code, and how a VirusTotal search surfaced what appears to be the first Mac malware sample built natively for Apple Silicon. That sample, a variant of a known family, had been submitted by a user of an open-source tool.

Before analyzing it, the presenter covers the arm64 essentials a reverser needs: general purpose registers and their 32-bit halves, the calling convention that passes early arguments in x0 through x7, the link register, the load and store model, condition flags and branch types. A short Objective-C hello world program ties these ideas to real disassembly. The malware resists decompilation because its code is padded with junk instructions and spurious calls, so the analysis relies on reading assembly directly.

The sample carries several anti-analysis checks. A ptrace call with the deny-attach flag makes it exit under a debugger; the talk bypasses this by breaking on the supervisor call and skipping it. The other checks, which look for disabled System Integrity Protection and for virtual machines, are identified by inspecting Objective-C message sends in a debugger, revealing that they shell out to a system utility and to a virtualization-detection script. The takeaway is that a modest arm64 foundation is enough to get past anti-analysis, after which passive process and file monitors can show what the sample actually does.

talks.title: Apple's Envy: Root once, bypass TCC
talks.teaser: Shows how root access on macOS can grant arbitrary apps TCC permissions such as Full Disk Access without user prompts.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common position: an attacker has root on a Mac but still cannot reach protected data. macOS layers mandatory controls on top of root, including System Integrity Protection and the Transparency, Consent and Control (TCC) system, which stores permissions in SQLite databases. The speaker reviews older shortcuts, such as enabling remote login over SSH to inherit Full Disk Access, and explains why Apple closed them in later releases.

The core technique avoids the user interface and consent prompts. A new admin user is created from the command line with the directory service tool, and remote management is enabled through the ARD kickstart command. On Big Sur, default deny entries in the system TCC database block the screen sharing agent from capturing the screen or posting keyboard events, so the speaker removes those entries. A local script then drives the desktop over a loopback VNC session, skips the setup assistant, and grants Terminal Full Disk Access through the privacy panel.

The talk closes by showing that GitHub Actions offers free macOS virtual machines for public repositories. A workflow can run the same steps and open a reverse tunnel for interactive access, giving researchers a test environment without owning a Mac. The practical takeaway is that a single root foothold may be enough to bypass TCC on the releases tested, and the speaker frames the work as use of existing behaviour rather than a new vulnerability.
